title: Gateway AI - Porting + Runtime Routing Workshop
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked the Gateway AI team through a parity mapping and runtime routing approach for porting endpoints from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood API. Discussion focused on API mapping, streaming and function-calling differences, KV cache behavior, batching, cost/latency trade-offs, and security controls (VPC/KMS/SAML). Agreed next steps: share parity matrix, run a 2-week pilot on Dedicated with a perf benchmark, and deliver security package.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-27
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Gateway CTO), Priya Raman (ML Engineer), Luis Ortega (Infra), Sam Lee (Product)

Auto-summary (generated): Quick parity workshop — mapping OpenAI/Together/TogetherAI model calls to Redwood API, talk through streaming vs chunked responses, KV cache implications, and routing policies for latency SLOs. Agreed to run a short pilot and share security artifacts.

Topics detected: parity-matrix, streaming, kv cache, dedicated capacity, vpc peering, kms, sso

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm jordan from redwood, i'm the ae on the account and with me is maya the solutions engineer. uh we'll run through a parity mapping and then show the console routing stuff, sound good?
[00:18] Ethan Cole: yep sounds good, thanks. i wanted to focus on the biggest lift — function calling and streaming differences — that's the crown jewel for our chat flows.
[00:35] Maya Singh: cool, we'll do a quick mapping table. first off, what's your current stack for inference? openai primarily, or mixtures?
[00:46] Priya Raman: mostly openai for prod, together for a few research endpoints, and we started a pilot with anthropic for safety-critical prompts — mix of all three.
[01:02] Luis Ortega: infra is k8s on gcp, some gpus in prod, but we want to push to dedicated infra or maybe redwood dedicated nodes, thinking about network egress too.
[01:18] Jordan Park: got it. so the parity checklist we'll share maps parameters like temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences, streaming websockets, and then more nuanced things — streaming chunk sizes, function calling semantics, and how you handle partial tokens when fallback occurs.
[01:40] Speaker 1: when you say fallback, do you mean automatic route to another model? like if capacity is busy?
[01:47] Maya Singh: exactly. redwood has routing policies — you can route by latency, cost, or region. simplest is primary model with a lower-cost fallback. tradeoffs: longer-context or bigger models as fallback can raise latency.
[02:04] Ethan Cole: okay, in our evaluation we need guaranteed 95th pct latency under 400ms for the main chat model, cost per 1k tokens is also a hard target.
[02:15] Jordan Park: perfect, that'll drive whether you pick hosted low-latency instances or dedicated pools. for parity with openai, most request/response params map 1:1 but function calling differs — we have structured output support and a stable json-path enforcement, but some clients need small prompt adjustments.
[02:36] Priya Raman: can you show the console where the routing policy is configured? and how do you eyeball token usage per route?
[02:46] Maya Singh: sure — jumping into the console. (screen share) here is the route graph, you can see traffic weights, fallback chains, and the per-model token breakdown over the last 24 hours. we also provide trace links to individual tokens, which helps track cost spikes.
[03:10] Jordan Park: note that console names and visuals vary; but we attach per-token cost estimates based on the model profile. we also show batching effectiveness so you can tune batch windows.
[03:24] Ethan Cole: that token trace looks useful. any gotchas for streaming where partials are cached? we saw at openai that partials sometimes get duplicated when reconnects happen.
[03:36] Maya Singh: yes. we do prefix/KV caching and we maintain idempotency tokens on streams to avoid dupes in reconnect. small caveat is with function calls and big nested args sometimes the streaming chunk boundaries need handling — our SDKs handle most but you'll want to test with your payload shapes.
[03:56] Luis Ortega: about the KV cache — if we have large retrieval contexts, is the cache shared across sessions or per-tenant?
[04:07] Maya Singh: cache is per-deployment; you can configure isolation per-customer or per-route. for your use case we'd recommend per-tenant segmentation in Dedicated so cached keys don't bleed.
[04:20] Sam Lee: what about quantization and perf — we looked at a togetherai 8-bit flavor, will redwood support q4/q8 and impact on output quality?
[04:31] Jordan Park: runtime supports quantized paths; we recommend running quality regression tests because q4 may slightly affect rare token probabilities. redwood optimize can suggest quantization profiles per workload.
[04:46] Ethan Cole: budget is important — can you ballpark cost delta moving from OpenAI to Redwood hosted vs dedicated?
[04:55] Jordan Park: quick high-level: hosted is typically higher unit cost but lower ops overhead; dedicated with reserved capacity reduces per-token costs especially at high throughput. we'll include an example with your traffic profile in the parity sheet.
[05:10] Priya Raman: okay. let's talk about function calling parity — our current openai flow relies on the 'function_call' automatic mode, does Redwood replicate that?
[05:20] Maya Singh: we have function-suggestion mode and explicit call mode. the mapping is one-to-one but our JSON schema validation for function args is stricter; that reduces downstream parsing errors but sometimes requires minor schema tweaks.
[05:36] Ethan Cole: any risk of semantic drift when we convert prompts? we have a lot of hand-tuned templates.
[05:45] Jordan Park: prompt translation tends to be minimal; we provide a small 'translation' layer and examples in the parity guide. occasionally tokenization differences require adjusting stop sequences.
[05:58] Speaker 1: do you support streaming with SSE and websockets? Together uses websockets heavily.
[06:07] Maya Singh: yes both; we also have resilient reconnect semantics and a server-sent events option for simpler clients. some of our customers use websockets for bi-directional data and sse for simpler streaming.
[06:22] Ethan Cole: security: we need KMS integration, SSO via SAML, and granular RBAC. also audit logs retained for 1 year.
[06:33] Jordan Park: we have KMS integrations for hosted & private, SAML SSO + SCIM provisioning, role-based access, and configurable audit log retention. for Dedicated and Private we can offer HSM attachments and custom retention policies.
[06:51] Luis Ortega: network wise will we need VPC peering? we prefer no public egress for sensitive UAT traffic.
[06:58] Maya Singh: for Private and Dedicated we support VPC peering and private endpoints. we'll document the exact CIDR ranges and egress rules in the security pack.
[07:11] Priya Raman: for the bench plan — we need to reproduce 99th percentile under sustained 200 rps and spike to 400 rps. can you run a parallel test harness?
[07:23] Maya Singh: yes — maya: we'll provide a test harness and sample load script. it measures latency distributions, token throughput, error rates, and billing estimates.
[07:34] Jordan Park: note that caching can distort latency — in the bench we'll include cold-start scenarios and warmed cache scenarios.
[07:42] Ethan Cole: good. what's the typical time to onboard a single endpoint to Dedicated? days, weeks?
[07:49] Jordan Park: usually 1-2 weeks to configure routing, models, and basic security for a simple endpoint; for VPC peering and SOC reviews add up to 2-4 weeks depending on your procurement.
[07:59] Sam Lee: procurement question — do you require enterprise contract for Dedicated?
[08:04] Jordan Park: Dedicated usually has a reserved capacity contract; pricing options vary monthly or yearly. we'll include draft T&Cs.
[08:12] Priya Raman: any notes on SDKs? our front-end devs use an openai-compatible wrapper — will they need to change code?
[08:21] Maya Singh: the SDKs are intentionally similar; we provide an adapter layer that matches openai's call shape for most cases. function calling and streaming may need small changes but minimal.
[08:34] Ethan Cole: what about vendor-specific rate limiting semantics? openai has bursts — do you throttle?
[08:42] Jordan Park: we provide soft rate limits and token quotas. Dedicated customers can set custom rate limits and elastic burst windows.
[08:50] Priya Raman: can you show an example parity mapping for an openai request to a redwood call?
[08:56] Maya Singh: sure, here's a quick snippet — (reads) replace model name mapping, map "max_tokens" to "response_max_tokens", attach "client_request_id" in metadata for traceability, and for streaming set "stream": true. also map function schemas to our strict json schema object.
[09:18] Speaker 1: sometimes transcripts cut mid-sentence, so apologies if i repeat.
[09:23] Maya Singh: no worries.
[09:26] Ethan Cole: about fallback routing — can you do regional fallbacks to reduce cross-region latency?
[09:33] Maya Singh: yes. you can configure region-aware routing with a primary region and a cross-region fallback, and you can bias by cost or latency.
[09:44] Luis Ortega: curious about billing granularity — per-token at aggregation level? we need per-team chargebacks.
[09:51] Jordan Park: billing reports include token-level breakdowns per-route and per-token class (prompt vs completion). you can export hourly CSVs and wire them into your chargeback system.
[10:02] Priya Raman: on error handling — openai had transient 5xx peaks; what's your retry/backoff recommendation?
[10:10] Maya Singh: client-side exponential backoff with idempotency keys; server provides clear error codes. we also support synchronous fallbacks to lighter models.
[10:19] Ethan Cole: okay great. let's switch to a quick demo of a parity mapping doc.
[10:25] Maya Singh: sharing a doc: parity-matrix.xlsx (link shared in chat). you'll see three columns: openai param, redwood param, notes/examples. here's a row for streaming chunk size.
[10:40] Jordan Park: one note — tokenization differences can change prompt token counts; we include a token delta estimator.
[10:47] Priya Raman: can the console auto-suggest routing weights to hit latencies? we have hundreds of endpoints.
[10:55] Maya Singh: yes, Optimize can suggest batching windows and routing weights based on observed latencies and cost goals. it produces a suggested rollout which you can apply gradually.
[11:09] Sam Lee: curious on rollouts — can we do canary at 5% then 25% then 100%?
[11:14] Maya Singh: yes built-in canary progressive rollout with automated rollback on quality regressions or latency breaches.
[11:22] Ethan Cole: how do you detect quality regressions? we use a prompt set and ground-truth answers.
[11:29] Maya Singh: Redwood Optimize supports evals tied to prompts and will alert on accuracy/semantic drift; you can tie alerts to automatic rollback.
[11:38] Jordan Park: quick product note — we also maintain model variant families for fallback so you don't have to retune prompts per-variant in many cases.
[11:46] Priya Raman: any pitfalls moving from togetherai where we ran custom kernels?
[11:52] Maya Singh: if you had custom kernel-level optimizations, some micro-behaviours might differ; we can run a diff bench. generally app-level parity is straightforward.
[12:02] Luis Ortega: ok jed — scheduling — we want a bench next week, and we'll provide traffic and sample payloads.
[12:09] Jordan Park: great. we'll action that.
[12:12] Ethan Cole: last thing — does redwood support offline on-prem package? for some gov data we need airgapped capability.
[12:20] Maya Singh: yes Private on-prem is available, requires a bit more lead time and an enterprise engagement.
[12:28] Jordan Park: wrapping up — i'll send parity-matrix, pricing, and schedule options. maya will own the bench plan. luis you'll share infra contact.
[12:37] Sam Lee: thanks all.
[12:40] Priya Raman: thanks.
[12:42] Ethan Cole: good session.
[12:44] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
